title: Cloud Computing

objectives.text: Use the NIST definition to classify a cloud offering by characteristic, service model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, FaaS) and deployment model, and name the five NIST cloud actors
Say who is responsible for each layer under the shared responsibility model for a given service model
Recognize the main cloud threats (misconfigured storage, IAM mistakes, metadata-service abuse, cryptojacking, log tampering) and map them to CSA Top Threats and MITRE ATT&CK
Describe an authorized cloud assessment, including provider testing rules, and match cloud security tools to their purpose
Read AWS CLI output to spot a public bucket, IMDSv1 still allowed or a long-term key, and name the AWS service that detects or prevents each issue
Explain Azure identity risks (managed identities, SAS tokens, consent phishing, standing admins) and the Entra controls that reduce them
Identify Google Cloud exposures (allUsers, service account keys, metadata tokens) and the matching controls
Use NIST SP 800-190 risk areas, Kubernetes and Docker ports, Pod Security Standards and RBAC to assess a container platform
Choose cloud defenses from CSA CCM, CIS Benchmarks, CSPM, CWPP, CASB and organization guardrails

readingMap.why: Service and deployment models, NIST actors and shared responsibility underpin every other question in the module.
Scenario questions ask you to name the threat or attack from its symptoms, including EC-Council's attack names.
Know the assessment flow, provider testing rules and which tool does what; skip step-by-step attack material.
S3 exposure, IMDSv2, IAM keys and CloudTrail/GuardDuty are the most concrete cloud items and appear as command-output questions.
Learn the IMDS header, managed identities, SAS types and the Entra controls; tool names at recognition level.
allUsers vs allAuthenticatedUsers, the metadata header and service account keys are the testable points.
Ports, privileged containers, Kubernetes Secrets, RBAC and the container tools are frequent exam material.
Countermeasure questions: pick the framework, benchmark, product family or guardrail that fits the scenario.

labs.name: Work through the flAWS challenge levels
labs.skill: Recognizing common AWS misconfigurations (public buckets, leaked keys, metadata exposure) in a hosted, legal environment

labs.name: Deploy a CloudGoat scenario in your own AWS account, then audit it with Prowler or ScoutSuite
labs.skill: Reading posture findings and IAM policies on a vulnerable-by-design lab you own; tear it down afterwards

labs.name: Scan images with Trivy and a local cluster with kube-bench
labs.skill: Finding image CVEs, secrets and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark failures on your own kind or minikube cluster

labs.name: Kubernetes Goat scenarios on a local cluster
labs.skill: Seeing RBAC, secret and privileged-pod weaknesses in an intentionally vulnerable cluster you run yourself

feynmanPrompts: Explain the shared responsibility model to a manager who thinks moving to the cloud means the provider handles all security, using IaaS, PaaS and SaaS examples.
Explain how an SSRF flaw in a web app can lead to stolen cloud credentials through the metadata service, and why IMDSv2 or a required header stops most of it.
Explain why a container is a weaker security boundary than a virtual machine, and list the settings that make a Kubernetes pod safer.
